with_skill.expectation: Does not treat the Idempotency-Key header as a ratified standard - notes the IETF draft expired unratified, so TTL, mismatch and concurrency semantics must be explicitly designed and documented
Mentions row lock + SERIALIZABLE as the mechanism to promote only when a request spans external non-rollbackable calls, not for this case
Offers blocking for the bounded result and 202-plus-status-URL as the alternatives for synchronous callers and long-running effects respectively
Advises integrators to complete their retry logic well within the documented window
Names decorrelated jitter as the variant to promote when a tight user-facing deadline makes time-to-success outweigh fleet load
Excludes equal jitter and no-jitter from the recommended menu (equal jitter identified as the loser among jittered options; no jitter re-synchronizes the fleet into the original spike)
Quantifies the amplification risk: a 200-instance fleet each retrying a few times multiplies load on a struggling downstream several-hundred-fold while every instance looks reasonable in isolation
When pairing with a circuit breaker, states the stacking order Retry then CircuitBreaker then RateLimiter then Bulkhead
For call chains, propagates the remaining deadline downward with the request (relative timeouts on the wire) so no hop starts work exceeding what the top-level caller has left
Notes RFC 9110 defines method-level idempotency but says nothing about the Idempotency-Key retrofit, so 'per the HTTP spec' does not cover these endpoints

without_skill.expectation: Recommends event-derived key derivation as the default (a key built from an identifier the caller already holds, e.g. their own transfer or order id)
Presents derivation options as a ranking - event-derived over request-scoped over a random UUID reused across retries - not an unordered list
Specifies that the same key arriving with a different request body is rejected with a conflict (409), never silently replayed
Makes or demands an explicit decision whether a stored failure replays verbatim or the operation is re-attempted without side effects (the Stripe v1 vs v2 fork)
Does not treat the Idempotency-Key header as a ratified standard - notes the IETF draft expired unratified, so TTL, mismatch and concurrency semantics must be explicitly designed and documented
Removes the Redis option from the menu entirely (or requires fencing tokens layered on top if Redis were unavoidable) rather than ranking it last as a fallback
Mentions row lock + SERIALIZABLE as the mechanism to promote only when a request spans external non-rollbackable calls, not for this case
Diagnoses the root cause as a binary seen/not-seen key model with no representation of an in-flight request
Defaults the in-flight response to a conflict (409) telling the caller to wait and retry
Requires the in-flight conflict and the payload-mismatch conflict to carry distinct machine-readable error codes
States that in-flight conflict and completed replay are different responses by design, never fallbacks of each other
Allows takeover of an abandoned request only after a lock timeout, via an atomic conditional update on the lock timestamp
Recommends an active completer background job that pushes abandoned in-flight requests through to completion, not passive expiry
Recommends a reaper job that deletes expired records and logs what it could not finish for a human
Splits retention into two horizons: a replay window governing correctness and a longer reaper threshold governing operational recovery
Explains the reaper threshold keeps failed records alive for human recovery (e.g. a Friday incident's failed requests surviving the weekend)
States a key reused after the replay window is treated as a brand-new request, not answered with an error
Requires the stored record to hold the full response verbatim (status and body) so the replay is indistinguishable from the original
Requires the replay window published to integrators as a concrete number, with the post-expiry behavior spelled out
Advises integrators to complete their retry logic well within the documented window
Treats the in-window duplicate side-effect rate as a zero-by-definition alarm on regression, not a threshold to tune
Treats 500 separately from the allowlist - retried cautiously, since some 500s are real bugs that fail identically on retry
Names decorrelated jitter as the variant to promote when a tight user-facing deadline makes time-to-success outweigh fleet load
Excludes equal jitter and no-jitter from the recommended menu (equal jitter identified as the loser among jittered options; no jitter re-synchronizes the fleet into the original spike)
Requires logging every retry with attempt number, error, and next wait
Points integrators at an established retry library (tenacity, Resilience4j, or equivalent) ahead of hand-rolled formulas
Quantifies the amplification risk: a 200-instance fleet each retrying a few times multiplies load on a struggling downstream several-hundred-fold while every instance looks reasonable in isolation
Names the token-bucket retry-quota implementation with its figures: 14 tokens per transient-error retry, 5 per throttle retry
Sets single-attempt timeouts at 2-3x measured p99 latency, never an OS default or a round number
When pairing with a circuit breaker, states the stacking order Retry then CircuitBreaker then RateLimiter then Bulkhead
For call chains, propagates the remaining deadline downward with the request (relative timeouts on the wire) so no hop starts work exceeding what the top-level caller has left
Notes RFC 9110 defines method-level idempotency but says nothing about the Idempotency-Key retrofit, so 'per the HTTP spec' does not cover these endpoints
Grounds the checklist in the fact that no ratified standard exists, so this documentation is the integrators' only normative source
